Field notes 09 · 26 August 2026

Neither trust nor control

A yes was true the day it was given. Nobody confirmed it again.

The phone rings before six. “Boss, they have not made the changes. We cannot start production.” Three weeks ago they confirmed they would be ready.

By eight he is writing the meeting invitation. A big one, with senior names in the room. Everyone in that location is going to understand what this delay costs. He wants to escalate high and pauses over the list of names. Which boss? The one above him, or the person who is not called a boss but decides anyway? He has never been sure how that place really works.

He goes through the three weeks again and again, and finds only one answer. They said they would be ready, and they did not deliver. No one even called to warn him. He keeps coming back to the same sentence: I trusted them. His trust was real. Professional adults, people who know their job better than he does. You do not stand over people like that and check on them every day. In his world, leaving them alone was the respect they had earned.

On their side the story is different, and it is just as reasonable. Three weeks ago somebody said yes, and that day it was true. Then things changed, the way they change every week. The plan was rebuilt around what was most urgent, day after day, because in their world that is what good management looks like. You steer every day. To them, the old yes was not a broken promise but a direction that no one had confirmed again. They read his silence the way he now reads their delay: if it still mattered, he would have called.

He trusted them. For three weeks, that trust meant not talking to them. Next time, he tells himself, he will check on them every day. But control is not the answer. Trust has a different job. Trust makes it easier to ask again, and easier to say that things have changed. It does not replace the conversation.

Anna Chodynicka, DRIFT Partners · First published 26 August 2026
